notes:
I've researched Zechariah 14 and written notes verse by verse below. The biggest split runs through the whole chapter. One side reads it as literal future events: Christ comes back to the Mount of Olives and then reigns for 1,000 years on earth (the premillennial view). The other side reads it as picture-language for the gospel age and the end of the world (the amillennial view, along with the older "spiritual" readings).

**What I couldn't find:** anything usable on bibleodyssey.org, oca.org (Orthodox) or any Pentecostal or Lutheran source on this chapter, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings. The site doesn't tell you who belongs to which church. Where I name someone's tradition (Calvin as Reformed, Gill as Baptist, Wesley as Methodist), that label is mine, not the source's.

**Overview: the main disagreement**
- **Literal and premillennial.** Guzik says Jesus will really return with His feet on the Mount of Olives, not as a symbol, and Jerusalem becomes the capital of the millennial earth. Jesus will literally return with His feet on the Mount of Olives—not a spiritual or symbolic event, but a material return to a material earth https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-14/ Walvoord treats the splitting of the Mount of Olives as one of the changes to the earth at the start of the millennium. Important changes will also occur on the face of the earth at the beginning of the millennium such as the division of the Mount of Olives (Zech 14:3-8). https://bible.org/seriespage/future-work-christ-%E2%80%94-part-iv-millennial-kingdom-and-eternal-state
- **Symbolic (Reformed).** Ligonier calls this perhaps the most symbolic chapter of the prophet's entire work. It sees the chapter pointing to the final battle and the new heavens and earth, not a 1,000-year reign. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-will-be-king
- **Fully figurative (Ellicott).** No event in history matches the chapter, so Ellicott reads all of it in a figurative, Messianic sense. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- **Fulfilled in the gospel age.** Coffman (Church of Christ) says Christ has already touched his feet down upon the mount of Olives. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/14-4.html GotQuestions explains that amillennialists see v. 4 fulfilled when Jesus taught on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24). https://www.gotquestions.org/amillennialism.html
- **Precept Austin's criticism.** The site argues that amillennialists have to turn these prophecies into symbols. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah-14-commentary
- **Lutheran note.** Precept Austin points out that Luther wrote two commentaries on Zechariah and stopped at the end of chapter 13 without explaining why. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah-14-commentary

---

**v. 1**
- Ellicott translates it "a day cometh *for* the Lord," a day when He shows His glory. The first thing that happens on that day is judgment on Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- **Disputed:** Benson reads this as the Romans destroying the unbelieving Jews. Gill says it is not Christ's first coming or the Roman judgment, but His later coming to convert the Jews. Another commentator on the same page says the literal reading must be given up: the chapter pictures God's kingdom being tested, growing and winning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-1.htm
- Gill also says the plunder is Jerusalem's own goods, divided by the enemy. He rejects the Targum's reading that it is the nations' goods divided by Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-1.htm
- Precept Austin sees a "divine reversal" in v. 14: the goods taken from Israel here are paid back. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61993/

**v. 2**
- The Pulpit Commentary says God uses the nations to refine His people. It argues the verse can't be about Rome, because a remnant stays in the city. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-2.htm
- Ellicott quotes Josephus on how the Romans killed or enslaved the people in AD 70, and asks where a remnant could have been. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- Guzik agrees: AD 70 had none of the rescue that follows in this chapter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-14/
- **Disputed:** Poole takes "all nations" to mean the Roman Empire. Gill instead points to the kings gathered at Armageddon (Revelation 16:14). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-2.htm
- Klein (New American Commentary) says the women of Zion will not escape this cruelty in the final battle. The Moody Bible Commentary says God is directing even these events toward a good end. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah-14-commentary

**v. 3**
- Calvin says "as He fights in the day of battle" covers all of God's past rescues of His people, not just the Red Sea. The verse gives the Church confidence till the end of the world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/zechariah/14.htm
- Ellicott: in Israel's worst hour God appears as their champion, as He did in the past. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- Guzik quotes Deane: God "goes forth" when He rescues His people and punishes their enemies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-14/

**v. 4**
- **Literal:** Guzik says this is Jesus, as God the Son, coming back in body to the Mount of Olives. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-14/ Precept Austin quotes Feinberg comparing it to the real parting of the Red Sea. It also cites a NET Bible note: the earthquake opens an escape route from Jerusalem. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah-14-commentary
- A note on Biblehub links this to Acts 1:11 and an old tradition that the Lord will return to the place He left from. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-4.htm
- **Symbolic:** Ligonier says God is spirit and has no physical feet, which shows the language is symbolic. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-will-be-king Ellicott calls the language figurative and notes that earthquakes often go with God's appearing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- **Other readings:** Clarke linked the split to Roman siege works on the mountain. Precept Austin calls that close to absurd. Coffman saw it as the gospel dividing the human race. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah-14-commentary

**v. 5**
- Ellicott makes several points:
  - Luther's translation "flee before" doesn't fit the Hebrew.
  - "Azal" may be a place near Jerusalem, or may simply mean "very near."
  - Mentioning Uzziah's earthquake doesn't date the prophecy.
  - "Holy ones" is better read as "angels."
  - "With thee" (some versions) shows the prophet's own joyful expectation.
  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- Guzik: the holy ones are the armies of heaven in Revelation 19:14. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-14/
- Precept Austin: they include both angels and believers who have died. Because the verse begins with another "then," it describes a second "coming," after the one in v. 3. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61993/
- An editor's note in Calvin's commentary reads "with thee" as God marching as Jerusalem's ally. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/zechariah/14.htm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott translates it: there shall be no light, and the heavenly bodies will fail. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html

**v. 7**
- The Pulpit Commentary: only God knows what kind of day it is and when it comes (Matthew 24:36). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-7.htm
- Keil: the stars losing their light matches other prophecies of the day of judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-7.htm
- Ellicott: as the darkest hour comes before dawn, God's saving light breaks out at evening. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- Guzik: the lights we steer our lives by will fade, but God will set up His own light. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-14/

**v. 8**
- **Literal:** Guzik sees a real river that flows all year, possibly the one in Ezekiel 47. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-14/
- **Spiritual:**
  - Wesley's Notes: the waters are the life-giving truths of the gospel, and "Jerusalem" is the Church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/14-8.html
  - Matthew Henry: fulfilled when the Spirit was poured out on the apostles in Jerusalem and the gospel went out to the nations. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zec/Zec_014.cfm
  - Calvin: water is a picture of the Holy Spirit, who both cleanses and waters. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment2/v1.0/harry/comm_vol30/htm/iii.xv.ix.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says hills higher than the city surround Jerusalem, so the waters can't physically flow as described. https://biblehub.com/zechariah/14-8.htm
- Ligonier: the year-round flow shows this life is eternal. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-will-be-king
- **Catholic and early church:**
  - Haydock's Catholic commentary says the living waters are the gospel. It adds that the Gentile converts outnumber the Jewish ones as much as the Mediterranean outsizes the Dead Sea. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/14-8.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary quotes Jerome: the waters keep flowing in peace and in persecution. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-14.html
  - A Biblehub article says Jerome also connected this verse to the water flowing from Christ's pierced side. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_living_waters_in_Zech_14_8.htm

**v. 9**
- Calvin: God can only be truly worshipped when He alone is supreme. The verse quietly condemns superstition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/zechariah/14.htm
- Keil: this means the kingdom of grace, not the kingdom of nature. Gill: Christ's spiritual reign in the latter days, when the nations become Christian. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-9.htm
- Ellicott: in context the verse means "all the land," but it can have a wider meaning. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- MacArthur (quoted by Precept Austin): there will be only one religion in the world during the millennium. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah-14-commentary

**v. 10**
- Ellicott explains the place names (Geba to Rimmon covers Judah from north to south). He reads Jerusalem being "raised up" as a picture of its religious importance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- Guzik: the mountains around the city are no longer needed for defence, so they can be flattened. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-14/
- Ligonier warns against a "woodenly literal" reading. It sees a picture of a city that is completely secure. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/worship-jerusalem
- Calvin: a new Jerusalem as large and splendid as the old one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/zechariah/14.htm

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: "utter destruction" is better translated "ban" (compare Revelation 22:3). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- Calvin: the city will be full of people again. He links this to the kingdom of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/zechariah/14.htm
- Guzik: Jerusalem will be safe for the first time in a long while. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-14/

**v. 12**
- Calvin: God's hidden vengeance reaches right inside a person, and nothing escapes it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/zechariah/14.htm
- Guzik notes that some people link the rotting flesh to nuclear weapons. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-14/
- Precept Austin: in time, vv. 12–15 come right after v. 3. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61993/

**v. 13**
- Ellicott hears echoes of earlier panics sent by God in Israel's history, such as 1 Samuel 14:20. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- Guzik's Ezekiel 38 commentary groups this verse with the defeat of Gog. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/

**v. 14**
- **Wording dispute:** Should it read Judah fights "at" or "against" Jerusalem? The Pulpit Commentary calls "against" (the Latin Vulgate's reading) a mistake. The Cambridge Bible lists three ways the enemy is destroyed: plague, killing each other, and Judah's attack. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-14.htm Ellicott also calls Ewald's "against" reading wrong. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- Barnes sees Judah working alongside God, and quotes "God made thee without thee; He doth not justify thee without thee." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-14.htm
- Gill reads the gathered wealth as the riches of the Papists falling to Christ's followers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-14.htm

**v. 15**
- Ellicott compares this to Achan's animals being destroyed with him (Joshua 7:24). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- Benson compares it to the plagues of Egypt. Matthew Henry: animals often suffer because of human sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-14.htm

**v. 16**
- Ellicott: the judgment is meant to heal. The feast is described in Old Testament terms and is not literal. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- Poole: the verse foretells converted Gentiles worshipping faithfully. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-16.htm
- Guzik: in the millennium the nations will come to Jerusalem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-14/
- Bible.org (Utley): foreigners were already welcome at this feast (Deuteronomy 16:14). https://bible.org/seriespage/zechariah-14
- Constable links the feast to Peter's offer of booths at the Transfiguration. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/14-16.html
- Ligonier: the feast stands for relying on God alone. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/worship-jerusalem

**v. 17**
- Ellicott: people can still fall away, and the punishment is described in picture-language. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- The Pulpit Commentary: "rain" means God's grace being held back. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-14.html
- Guzik: God won't force anyone to worship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-14/
- Feinberg (quoted by Precept Austin): the need for rain shows this is the millennium, not the eternal state. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61993/

**v. 18**
- Ellicott: the usual translation is impossible here. He suggests reading it as a question, or dropping the "not" as the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) does. He also argues the rain penalty shows the verse isn't meant literally. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- Matthew Henry: Egypt doesn't need rain, but people who can live without rain still can't live without God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zec/Zec_014.cfm

**v. 19**
- Keil translates it "the sin of Egypt." He says it doesn't mean pagans will still exist then; it means paganism will have no place in God's kingdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-16.htm

**v. 20**
- Ellicott: the words on the high priest's headband appear even on horses' bells. Everything is raised to a higher level of holiness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- Guzik: horses are no longer needed for war. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-14/
- A sermon on Biblehub applies it to ordinary daily work: Holy men make all things holy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-20.htm

**v. 21**
- **Sacrifices disputed:**
  - Guzik: animal sacrifice will go on in the millennium, but not to pay for sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-14/
  - Ellicott: this is not a promise that the Mosaic ritual will return. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
  - Gill: the sacrifices are spiritual ones, prayer and praise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-21.htm
- **"Canaanite":** Barnes says it means people who belong to Israel outwardly but not truly. The Geneva Bible notes say there will be no hypocrites. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/14-21.htm Ellicott says it means a foreigner or unbeliever. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-14.html
- Matthew Henry: one place and one vessel will be as acceptable to God as another. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zec/Zec_014.cfm
